papers.finding: Peer support relieves depressive symptoms significantly better than usual care.
papers.detail: 7 randomised trials with 869 participants. Compared with group cognitive behavioural therapy, there was no significant difference.

einordnung.title: Shared lived experience
einordnung.text: People with similar experiences support each other as equals, based on empathy and mutual help (Penney, 2018a).

einordnung.title: A complement, not a replacement
einordnung.text: Peer support does not replace medical, therapeutic or psychological treatment. It complements it.

einordnung.title: A biopsychosocial view
einordnung.text: Health as the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors (Engel, 1977). Low-threshold services are often missing, especially when it comes to social integration.

einordnungText: Peer support refers to a process in which people with shared experiences or similar health or social challenges come together as equals to support one another (Penney, 2018a). A peer is a person on an equal footing with a similar life situation, social background or experience (of illness). Support describes a relationship based on empathy, encouragement and mutual help (Penney, 2018a).

In Switzerland, the term peer is not yet protected or uniformly defined. Accordingly, peer support is understood and implemented differently in practice and research. The literature describes various peer approaches, including peer support, peer education, peer coaching and peer counselling, which differ in their objectives, understanding of roles, proximity to professional services and degree of structure (Dennis, 2003; Solomon, 2004).

Shared lived experience is central to all peer approaches. Peer support is not based on diagnostic models or professional roles, but on empathic understanding through shared burdens and challenges (Mead et al., 2001). The exchange takes place on an equal footing and deliberately differs from traditional therapeutic services.
Peer support does not replace medical, therapeutic or psychological treatment. At restful too, it is understood as a complementary form of support that meaningfully adds to professional care.

Historically, the peer approach did not originate in conventional medicine but in the self-help, civil rights and recovery movements. From the 1930s onwards, the first organised forms of mutual support emerged, for example in self-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous. The core idea was that shared experience is a form of knowledge in its own right and should not be seen merely as a deficit (Borkman, 1976; Penney, 2018b). From the 1980s and 1990s, peer support was increasingly described scientifically and grounded in theory as a reciprocal support process based on equality and empowerment (Penney, 2018b; Solomon, 2004).

At restful, we follow the biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1977), which sees health as the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors. Switzerland has high-quality medical and therapeutic care. At the same time, research and practice show that complementary, low-threshold services are lacking, particularly in continuous psychosocial support, coping with everyday life and social integration. We therefore see digital peer support as a preventive complement to existing care.
